paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the structure underlying an exchangeable graph model, a family that includes several popular network models. That structure is represented by a mathematical object called a graphon. The central challenge is to construct an estimator that is computationally practical and has a proof that its estimates become accurate as the available information grows.

The proposed solution is a histogram estimator built through a sorting-and-smoothing procedure. It first orders the graph according to empirical node degrees, giving the observed network an organized arrangement. It then smooths the sorted graph using total variation minimization. These two stages turn the estimation problem into a concrete computational procedure rather than leaving consistency as an abstract statistical objective.

The authors prove consistency using sparsity ideas from compressed sensing and describe the estimator as numerically efficient. The contribution connects a simple sequence of operations with a formal statistical guarantee. This makes sorting and smoothing a theoretically supported approach to graphon estimation within the paper’s framework.
icml-2014-a-consistent-histogram-estimat.tldr: A sorting-and-smoothing algorithm provides a numerically efficient, provably consistent histogram estimator of graphons.

paragraphs: The paper asks when combining pairwise comparisons will recover an optimal overall ranking. It assumes that comparisons are drawn randomly and independently from an underlying probability distribution. Within that setting, it compares algorithms by the statistical conditions sufficient for their convergence, making the data-generating assumptions central to the analysis.

Rank centrality and least squares ranking converge under a time-reversibility, or Bradley–Terry–Luce, condition. A matrix form of Borda count works under a strictly more general low-noise condition. Interestingly, maximum likelihood estimation based on the Bradley–Terry–Luce model also succeeds under that broader condition. Its convergence therefore does not require the data distribution to satisfy the narrower assumption used to construct the estimator.

The authors introduce an SVM-based ranking method with a guarantee under an even more general condition, called generalized low-noise. They provide explicit sample complexity bounds for exact recovery in every case. Experiments support the theoretical findings, helping explain how different ranking procedures behave under different statistical assumptions.
icml-2014-a-statistical-convergence-pers.tldr: The paper identifies progressively broader statistical conditions under which pairwise ranking algorithms recover an optimal ranking.

paragraphs: Algorithmic leveraging reduces a large matrix problem by sampling and rescaling data using statistical leverage scores. The paper examines what this reduction does to parameter estimation in linear regression. Its focus is statistical accuracy: a sampling method can have strong computational guarantees while still affecting the bias and variance of the resulting estimates.

The authors derive bias and variance results for several sampling variants, both conditional on the observed data and without that conditioning. They find that neither leverage-based nor uniform sampling dominates the other by these statistical criteria. This contrasts with the uniformly stronger worst-case algorithmic guarantees associated with leverage-based sampling and shows why the two perspectives can lead to different judgments.

The analysis motivates two new methods. SLEV uses adjusted, or shrunk, leverage scores to form a smaller least-squares problem. LEVUNW instead solves a smaller unweighted problem. Empirical results indicate that the theory predicts practical behavior and that the new methods improve performance in the reported evaluations.
icml-2014-a-statistical-perspective-on-a.tldr: Analyzing sampling through regression bias and variance reveals tradeoffs that motivate two improved leveraging algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper develops an optimization framework for regularized loss minimization, a formulation shared by several major machine learning methods. Its starting point is stochastic dual coordinate ascent. The contribution concerns how to solve these learning problems more efficiently, with the same framework covering several different objectives.

The authors introduce a proximal version of the method and then accelerate it through an inner–outer iteration procedure. This places the underlying optimization method inside a larger iterative scheme. The two contributions are connected: the proximal formulation supplies the method to be accelerated, while the nested procedure supplies the acceleration mechanism analyzed in the paper.

Runtime analysis yields improved rates over the stated state of the art for SVMs, logistic regression, ridge regression, Lasso, and multiclass SVMs. Experiments validate the theoretical findings. The breadth of this list matters because it spans several regularized learning formulations, making the result a reusable optimization framework rather than an improvement confined to a single prediction model.
icml-2014-accelerated-proximal-stochasti.tldr: A proximal dual coordinate ascent framework uses nested iterations to improve runtime rates for several standard learning problems.

paragraphs: Detecting multiple objects can require human expertise when automatic detectors are insufficient, but expert annotation is expensive. The paper treats the timing of human involvement as part of the detection problem. The goal is to obtain strong detection performance while making careful use of limited supervision.

For a rich class of base detectors, the authors formulate a sequential decision problem that determines when to request expert help. They show that its objective satisfies adaptive submodularity, a mathematical property that supports performance guarantees for their algorithm. This connects a practical allocation question—where human effort is most useful—to a formal analysis of decisions made as information arrives.

The method is demonstrated on three real-world tasks, including biodiversity monitoring using micro UAVs in the Sumatra rain forest. Active detection outperforms its passive counterpart in the reported results. On certain tasks, it also substantially outperforms straightforward applications of existing active learning methods, supporting the value of a decision procedure designed specifically for detection.
icml-2014-active-detection-via-adaptive-.tldr: A sequential approach to requesting expert supervision gives active object detection theoretical guarantees and strong results on three real-world tasks.

paragraphs: The paper first addresses optimization of strongly convex composite functions when the parameters describing their convexity are unknown. Such information matters for achieving fast convergence. The proposed adaptive accelerated proximal gradient method uses restarting to estimate the strong convexity parameter automatically and achieves nearly optimal iteration complexity.

The authors then consider high-dimensional least squares with an ℓ1 penalty. This objective is not strongly convex overall, so the first result cannot simply be applied on that basis. However, it has restricted strong convexity over sparse vectors. The approach uses this more limited structure by combining the adaptive method with a homotopy continuation scheme that generates a sparse solution path toward optimality.

The combined method achieves global linear convergence and an iteration bound with weaker dependence on the restricted condition number than previous work. The key connection is between the path followed by the algorithm and the region where useful curvature is available. Sparsity therefore supports both the target solution and the convergence analysis.
icml-2014-an-adaptive-accelerated-proxim.tldr: Adaptive restarting and a sparse continuation path yield fast convergence without requiring known convexity parameters.

paragraphs: The paper examines the computational expense of Bayesian posterior sampling on large datasets. A standard Metropolis–Hastings test can require evaluating the likelihood across all observations just to decide whether to accept or reject one proposed sample. The authors question whether that much computation is necessary for every binary decision.

They replace the exact acceptance rule with an approximate rule based on a sequential hypothesis test. This allows an acceptance or rejection decision to be reached with high confidence using only a fraction of the data required by the exact rule. Reducing the work per decision makes it possible to generate more samples within the same amount of computing time.

The approximation introduces asymptotic bias, so the gain comes with a real statistical tradeoff. The authors show that this bias can be controlled and that reduced variance from drawing more samples per unit of time more than offsets it in their analysis. The result evaluates sampling accuracy together with computational cost rather than considering exactness alone.
icml-2014-austerity-in-mcmc-land-cutting.tldr: An approximate Metropolis–Hastings test uses less data per decision, trading controlled bias for more samples and reduced variance.

paragraphs: Forecasting several steps ahead presents a choice between reusing a one-step model recursively and fitting a separate model for each forecast horizon. The two strategies involve different balances of bias and estimation variance. The paper emphasizes that choosing between them becomes still harder when nonlinear machine learning models enter the picture.

The proposed strategy combines the two approaches. It begins with traditional recursive linear forecasts and boosts them using a direct strategy, with a boosting autoregression procedure applied at each horizon. This retains a shared recursive starting point while allowing the forecast for each horizon to receive its own adjustment. The method therefore addresses the tradeoff through a combined construction.

The authors examine bias and variance using simulated time series, then evaluate forecasting performance on real series from two competitions. They report excellent overall performance relative to standard forecasting strategies. These findings support the combined approach in the evaluated settings, while the decomposition helps explain its behavior beyond a single aggregate error comparison.
icml-2014-boosting-multi-step-autoregres.tldr: Horizon-specific boosting improves recursive linear forecasts by combining recursive and direct forecasting strategies.

paragraphs: The paper addresses nearest neighbor search when enormous numbers of queries must be processed. It combines k-d trees, which organize data through hierarchical subdivision, with GPUs, which provide substantial parallel computing capacity. A direct combination performs poorly because conditional computation and inefficient memory access interfere with effective use of the hardware.

The proposed buffer k-d tree changes the classical data structure so that the search can be reorganized. The important design question is how to preserve the useful subdivision provided by the tree while arranging computation in a way that suits a many-core device. The contribution therefore concerns the coordination of a search structure with its execution on parallel hardware.

Experiments show that the approach can benefit from both hierarchical subdivision and the GPU’s computational resources. An astronomy application demonstrates its potential for workloads involving hundreds of millions of nearest neighbor queries. This application illustrates why reorganizing the search matters: efficient processing must hold across a very large volume of queries.
icml-2014-buffer-k-d-trees-processing-ma.tldr: Buffer k-d trees reorganize nearest neighbor search to better combine hierarchical indexing with GPU computation.

paragraphs: The paper places persistent homology within a statistical estimation framework. Its question is how persistence diagrams computed from random data relate to the topology of the underlying source of those data. This shifts attention from computing a diagram for one sample to understanding how that diagram behaves as an estimate.

The authors establish convergence rates for diagrams associated with observations randomly sampled from any compact metric space. The estimates converge toward a well-defined limit diagram encoding topological features of the sampling distribution’s support. The target is therefore a property of the underlying space occupied by the distribution, giving the statistical analysis a precise object to recover.

The argument uses a stability result for persistence to connect diagram estimation with support estimation measured through Gromov–Hausdorff distance. This connection allows geometric estimation results to inform the accuracy of topological summaries. Numerical experiments in several settings illustrate the theory. The contribution provides rates of convergence, going beyond a qualitative claim that more data should improve the diagrams.
icml-2014-convergence-rates-for-persiste.tldr: Persistence diagrams receive statistical convergence guarantees by linking topological stability to estimation of a distribution’s support.

paragraphs: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process becomes difficult as the search space grows. Heuristics can reduce that space, but their computational value is hard to assess without theoretical bounds. This paper asks how to describe the part of the search space that remains reachable when heuristics guide planning.

The authors use covering numbers to characterize the size of that reachable space. This gives a way to connect the effectiveness of a heuristic with the complexity of the planning problem it leaves behind. The analysis also informs a practical algorithm, Packing-Guided Value Iteration, or PGVI. The theoretical characterization thus serves as a basis for algorithm design.

Empirically, PGVI is competitive with state-of-the-art point-based methods on 65 small benchmark problems and outperforms them on four larger problems. These results support the practical usefulness of the analysis in the tested settings. The distinction between small and larger benchmarks matters: the clearest reported advantage appears on the larger problems, where search-space size is especially consequential.
icml-2014-covering-number-for-efficient-.tldr: Covering-number analysis links heuristic effectiveness to POMDP planning complexity and motivates a competitive planning algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper develops a data-based representation of where NBA players choose to shoot. Informal descriptions of player styles can be intuitive but difficult to measure or compare systematically. The authors seek a compact account of spatial shooting habits that supports both comparisons between players and player-specific modeling.

They model shot attempts as a point process and use non-negative matrix factorization to obtain a low-dimensional representation of offensive player types. The resulting low-rank spatial decomposition summarizes shooting behavior through a smaller collection of patterns. This connects the locations of individual attempts to a representation of broader player tendencies learned without supervised type labels.

The discovered spatial representations correspond to intuitive descriptions of NBA player types. They can also be used to model other spatial effects, including shooting accuracy. The contribution is a common quantitative basis for describing shot selection and extending that description to related spatial questions. It gives measured structure to comparisons that otherwise depend on loosely specified impressions of player behavior.
icml-2014-factorized-point-process-inten.tldr: Point-process modeling and non-negative matrix factorization uncover compact spatial patterns that describe NBA players’ shooting habits.

paragraphs: The paper proposes scalable Bayesian regression through a mixture of Gaussian process experts. Each expert has its own inducing points, the compact representation used in sparse Gaussian process approximations. Data are assigned probabilistically according to proximity to the experts, making allocation an explicit part of the model.

This allocation supports fast variational inference for learning both inducing inputs and expert hyperparameters. The model is easy to parallelize and handles non-stationarity directly. With K experts, the method can achieve K² reductions in runtime and memory relative to popular sparse approaches such as FITC. This is a possible scaling advantage, distinct from the measured speedups in the experiments.

On datasets with around 10,000 training points, the method trains up to five times faster than FITC while attaining comparable accuracy. On a dataset with 100,000 training points, it substantially outperforms six competitive baselines with a few hours of training. These results support the practical value of combining local expert allocation with sparse approximation.
icml-2014-fast-allocation-of-gaussian-pr.tldr: Probabilistic allocation among sparse Gaussian process experts enables efficient inference and strong regression results on large datasets.

paragraphs: The paper develops a stochastic version of the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, aimed at combining inexpensive iterations with faster convergence. Existing stochastic methods have low per-iteration cost, while batch ADMM visits all samples during each iteration. The proposed method seeks the convergence rate of the batch approach without that repeated full-data work.

Its central mechanism incrementally approximates the full gradient within a linearized ADMM formulation. On convex problems, the convergence rate improves from O(1/√T) to O(1/T), where T counts iterations. This matches the stated batch ADMM rate while preserving low per-iteration complexity. The distinction matters because iteration count and the cost of each iteration jointly determine computational usefulness.

Experiments on graph-guided fused lasso show that the algorithm is significantly faster than the compared state-of-the-art stochastic and batch ADMM methods. The empirical finding complements the rate analysis: the proposed gradient approximation yields a practical speed advantage on the reported application as well as a stronger theoretical convergence rate.
icml-2014-fast-stochastic-alternating-di.tldr: Incremental gradient approximation gives stochastic ADMM an O(1/T) convex convergence rate with inexpensive iterations.

paragraphs: The paper studies a bandit problem in which reward distributions depend on both the chosen arm and an underlying type. Types organize those distributions into a small number of clusters. This adds hidden structure to the decision problem: selecting rewarding arms is connected to understanding which type or class governs the rewards.

The authors separate three levels of uncertainty. First, reward distributions are known and types share an underlying cluster, but the type’s identity is unknown. Next, types may belong to different classes, creating a more challenging problem. Finally, the reward distributions themselves are completely unknown. This progression distinguishes uncertainty about identity from uncertainty about the reward model.

For each setting, the paper introduces specific algorithms and derives nontrivial regret guarantees. Numerical experiments focus on the most challenging agnostic case and show excellent performance in several difficult scenarios. The contribution is therefore a set of methods matched to different available knowledge, together with theoretical and empirical evidence that the latent structure can be addressed.
icml-2014-latent-bandits-dfcb7e5f26.tldr: The paper develops bandit algorithms and regret guarantees for rewards organized by hidden types and clusters.

paragraphs: Choosing bundle prices requires understanding how much consumers value the items together. The relevant information is the joint distribution of their valuations, including how values for different items are related. The paper considers retailers who have individual-item sales transactions but cannot directly observe the consumer valuations behind those transactions.

The authors treat valuations as latent variables and fit a copula model for their correlated distribution. They develop an inference procedure that uses only the transaction records for individual items. This connects routinely observed purchase data with the unobserved joint valuation model needed for bundle pricing, making dependence between item valuations part of the inference task.

The procedure is statistically consistent and computationally tractable. Simulations and data experiments demonstrate consistency and scalability, while also showing the importance of incorporating correlations in the joint distribution. The findings support estimating relationships among valuations when building a model for bundle decisions. The contribution centers on recovering this pricing-relevant distribution from transactions rather than requiring direct observations of willingness to pay.
icml-2014-latent-variable-copula-inferen.tldr: A consistent, tractable copula inference method estimates correlated consumer valuations from individual-item sales transactions for bundle pricing.

paragraphs: The paper studies nonlinear classification in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space from two complementary directions. The primal task is to find a perfect separator when one exists. The dual task is to provide evidence that such a separator does not exist. The approach generalizes the Perceptron and Von Neumann algorithms.

The authors formulate classification as maximizing a regularized normalized hard margin. Using the representer theorem, they express the problem through a geometry determined by the kernel’s normalized, signed Gram matrix. For separable data, they derive an accelerated smoothed algorithm with a rate proportional to √log(n)/ρ, compared with the classical kernelized Perceptron’s 1/ρ² dependence, where ρ is the margin.

For the nonseparable case, an RKHS version of Gordan’s separation theorem supports an interpretation of negative margins. These results yield guarantees for a primal–dual algorithm that returns either a perfect separator when feasible or an approximate dual certificate of near-infeasibility. The framework thus addresses both successful separation and principled evidence about its absence.
icml-2014-margins-kernels-and-non-linear.tldr: A smoothed kernel classification framework accelerates separator search and provides approximate certificates when separation is nearly infeasible.

paragraphs: Scene labeling assigns a class to every pixel in an image. Good predictions require both accurate individual labels and coherent relationships across the image. A large surrounding image patch can provide the necessary context, but the paper seeks to capture long-range dependencies while limiting the model’s capacity.

The proposed recurrent convolutional network expands the context it considers through recurrence. As that context grows, the system identifies and corrects its own errors. It learns directly from raw pixels in an end-to-end procedure and does not require a separate segmentation technique or task-specific features. Recurrence therefore supplies a mechanism for incorporating wider spatial information within the learned system.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on the Stanford Background and SIFT Flow datasets, alongside fast test-time operation. These findings connect the architectural design to both labeling quality and inference cost. The contribution demonstrates that modeling complex spatial dependencies through recurrence can support accurate, visually coherent scene labeling without making inference expensive in the reported evaluations.
icml-2014-recurrent-convolutional-neural.tldr: A recurrent convolutional network expands spatial context to refine pixel labels while maintaining fast inference.

paragraphs: The paper studies how options can accelerate planning in Markov decision processes with continuous state spaces. Options are control structures that include both primitive actions and actions extending over time. The question is whether these longer actions can help approximate value iteration reach useful value estimates and policies in fewer iterations.

The convergence analysis identifies pessimistic initial value estimates as an important condition. Under that condition, options can speed convergence relative to planning with primitive actions alone, even when the extended actions are suboptimal and available only sparsely across the state space. The result shows that options need not themselves be ideal or widely distributed to provide a planning advantage.

Experiments on an optimal replacement task and a complex inventory management task demonstrate the potential for faster convergence in practice. Faster progress toward the optimal value function means better policies can be obtained with fewer iterations. The contribution therefore gives both a conditional theoretical explanation and practical examples of why temporally extended actions can help planning.
icml-2014-scaling-up-approximate-value-i.tldr: With pessimistic initial value estimates, even suboptimal and sparsely available options can accelerate approximate value iteration.

paragraphs: Binary classification ideally minimizes the number of incorrect predictions, but directly optimizing the nonconvex 0–1 loss is typically computationally intractable. A common alternative sums convex surrogate losses over individual examples. This paper revisits that construction by asking what properties a classification loss should satisfy at the level of the whole sample.

The authors propose an axiomatic framework and develop coherent loss as a tractable upper bound on empirical classification error across the dataset. They show that it gives a strictly tighter approximation than any convex cumulative loss approach while keeping the optimization problem convex. The significance is that a closer bound on the classification objective need not require giving up convex optimization.

The approach also admits a robustness interpretation that connects it to robust SVMs. Experiments show better performance than a standard SVM when additional constraints are imposed. That empirical qualification matters: the reported advantage concerns constrained settings. Together, the theoretical and experimental results motivate reconsidering how a classification surrogate combines information across training examples.
icml-2014-the-coherent-loss-function-for.tldr: Coherent loss provides a tighter convex upper bound on empirical classification error and improves on standard SVMs in constrained experiments.

paragraphs: The paper combines two ways of modeling annotated text. Multinomial inverse regression relates word distributions to metadata and response variables, but does not exploit corpus structure. Traditional topic models capture variation within a document collection but do not account for external variables. The goal is to bring these complementary sources of information together.

The inverse regression topic model is a mixed-membership extension of multinomial inverse regression. It incorporates topic structure while retaining the connection between word use and external variables. The authors provide an efficient batch estimation algorithm and an online version suitable for large corpora, giving the model two routes to practical inference.

Applications use 73,000 Congressional press releases and 150,000 Yelp reviews. The model outperforms both multinomial inverse regression and supervised topic models on prediction in these evaluations. Examples also demonstrate systematic discovery of lexical variation within topics, a capability the authors distinguish from previous supervised topic models. This adds an exploratory use alongside the predictive benefit.
icml-2014-the-inverse-regression-topic-m.tldr: The inverse regression topic model combines corpus structure with external variables to improve prediction and reveal word-use variation within topics.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes bandit problems where each decision combines basic arms into a complex action. Feedback may reveal only a function of their rewards, such as the maximum reward in a chosen subset. This creates coupling across actions, making their statistical relationship important to learning.

The authors prove a frequentist regret bound for Thompson sampling in a general framework of parameters, actions, observations, and likelihoods. The bound assumes a discretely supported prior, but does not require independent arms, conjugate priors, or closed-form posteriors. Regret grows logarithmically with time, with an improved constant that captures coupling induced by the reward structure.

Applications yield improved bounds for subset-selection problems, including the first nontrivial bounds reported for nonlinear maximum-reward feedback from subsets. Numerical studies examine subset selection and job scheduling, using particle filters when posterior distributions lack closed forms. The work connects a broad regret analysis with computation for problems whose feedback cannot be separated into individual arm rewards.
icml-2014-thompson-sampling-for-complex-.tldr: Thompson sampling receives logarithmic regret bounds that account for coupled feedback in complex bandit actions under discretely supported priors.

paragraphs: The paper studies online learning when the learner does not know how many rounds will occur. It distinguishes a randomly chosen horizon from one controlled by an adversary, using the known fixed-horizon problem as a starting point. This separation makes the source of uncertainty about stopping time part of the analysis.

For a random horizon with restricted losses, the authors derive a fully optimal minimax algorithm. For an adversarial horizon, they prove a lower bound showing that control over the stopping time gives the adversary strictly more power than a fixed, known horizon. Thus, uncertainty about duration can change the underlying worst-case learning problem.

The random-horizon solution motivates an adaptive algorithm that behaves as though the horizon came from a special distribution family. Regardless of how the actual horizon is chosen, it achieves the optimal worst-case regret rate. The framework can be combined with several online learning approaches, and experiments show improvements over many existing algorithms in online linear optimization.
icml-2014-towards-minimax-online-learnin.tldr: Minimax analysis of unknown stopping times motivates an adaptive online learner with an optimal worst-case regret rate.

paragraphs: The paper seeks to explain why latent Dirichlet allocation performs differently across datasets and tasks. Despite the model’s widespread use, the authors identify a shortage of formal guidance about which data properties affect inference. Their aim is to connect practical topic-modeling choices with a systematic statistical account of learning.

The analysis studies posterior contraction rates for topics as the amount of data increases. These rates describe how the posterior becomes concentrated around the topics being estimated. The resulting theorems characterize factors affecting LDA’s inferential performance, turning the broad question of whether more data helps into a more structured examination of how topic estimation improves.

A supporting empirical study uses synthetic data and real collections including news, web articles, and tweets. The authors use the theoretical and empirical results to offer guidance on selecting suitable datasets and specifying model parameters. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and practical: it links statistical analysis of topic recovery to decisions made when applying topic models.
icml-2014-understanding-the-limiting-fac.tldr: Posterior contraction analysis explains factors affecting LDA topic estimation and informs dataset and parameter choices.

paragraphs: The paper develops clustering models for high-dimensional observations on a unit sphere. It uses the von Mises–Fisher distribution as the basis for representing this data and aims to discover clusters that are more intuitive than those produced by existing approaches. The contribution is a suite of related models for different kinds of structure.

A Bayesian mixture allows information to be shared among clusters. A hierarchical mixture adds multiscale shrinkage and a tree-structured view of the data. A temporal mixture models how clusters evolve over time. These variants extend the clustering task beyond a single flat grouping, addressing relationships among groups and changes in their organization.

The authors develop fast variational inference methods and collapsed Gibbs sampling techniques for all three models. Experiments across six datasets provide strong empirical support relative to tools including K-means, multinomial mixtures, and latent Dirichlet allocation. The results support combining a spherical data model with Bayesian, hierarchical, or temporal structure in the evaluated clustering settings.
icml-2014-von-mises-fisher-clustering-mo.tldr: Bayesian, hierarchical, and temporal von Mises–Fisher mixtures provide structured clustering for high-dimensional spherical data.
